label: The Tensor Notation
notes: Chapter eighteen runs from printed page three hundred twenty-eight to three hundred forty-one and converts geometry into index bookkeeping. The aim is freedom from rectangular axes: oblique and curvilinear coordinates become routine once upper and lower indices, the metric, and the summation convention are in hand. Stress that indices are addresses, not exponents.

label: Upper and Lower Indices
notes: Open by separating the two component languages. Contravariant components are coefficients that build a vector along the basis, so they vary inversely with basis length. Covariant components are projections onto the basis. The placement of the index records which transformation law applies, and this single discipline prevents almost every mistake students make in oblique frames.

label: The Einstein Summation Convention
notes: Introduce the convention that a repeated index appearing once up and once down is silently summed over its range. Emphasise that the surviving free indices on both sides of an equation must match exactly. This is not mere shorthand; the up-down pairing encodes a genuine contraction that is invariant under change of coordinates.

label: Dual Bases
notes: Define the dual basis by the Kronecker condition, so each reciprocal vector is orthogonal to two primal vectors and scaled against the third. In three dimensions the cross-product formula divided by the Jacobian builds it explicitly. The notebook verifies the identity to machine precision, confirming the dual basis is the natural measuring frame for covariant components.

label: The Metric Tensor
notes: The fundamental tensor collects every inner product of basis vectors into a symmetric matrix. It is the device that lowers an index, turning contravariant components into covariant ones. Point out that the diagonal entries are squared basis lengths and off-diagonal entries measure obliqueness, so the metric is where all the geometry of the coordinate frame actually lives.

label: The Line Element
notes: Show the line element as the metric contracted twice with coordinate differentials. On a small coordinate parallelogram each side is a basis vector times a differential, and the squared diagonal expands into the sum of metric components. This is the master formula of the chapter; arc length, angle, and area all descend from it.

label: Raising and Lowering Indices
notes: Introduce the inverse metric as the contravariant tensor that raises an index, undoing what the metric lowered. The metric and its inverse contract to the Kronecker delta, the identity of tensor algebra. Stress that raising then lowering returns the original component exactly, which the notebook confirms through its reconstruction check at machine precision.

label: What Makes an Object a Tensor
notes: A tensor is defined by how its components transform under a coordinate change: each upper index brings a Jacobian factor and each lower index its inverse. Rank counts the indices. The point is that tensor equations hold in every coordinate system at once, which is precisely why the notation deserves the central role it plays here.

label: Reciprocal Lattices
notes: Make duality physical with the reciprocal lattice. The reciprocal basis is the inverse transpose of the direct basis, and its points are normals to families of equally spaced lattice planes. Note the inverse relation between direct spacing and reciprocal length, and mention that face-centred and body-centred cubic lattices are reciprocal up to scale.

label: General Coordinates and the Jacobian
notes: In curvilinear coordinates the basis vectors vary from point to point, being tangent to the coordinate curves. Cylindrical coordinates give the clean example: the metric is the diagonal one, r-squared, one, and the Jacobian equals r. The Jacobian is the local volume scale of the coordinate map, which the chapter will need for integration.

label: Christoffel Symbols and Covariant Derivatives
notes: Because the basis changes, an ordinary derivative of a vector field is not itself a tensor. The Christoffel symbols record how the basis turns, and adding their correction yields the covariant derivative, which is tensorial. This is the bridge from static index algebra to the differential geometry of surfaces that the following chapters develop.

label: The Alternating Symbol and Recap
notes: Close with the alternating symbol, which writes determinants and oriented volume as a contraction: plus one for even permutations, minus one for odd, zero on repeats. Recap the survival kit: dual bases, the metric, the line element, raising and lowering, the transformation law, and covariant differentiation, all consistent index hygiene.
